title: K Closest Points to Origin
description:
# K Closest Points to Origin

Given points `points[i] = [xi, yi]` on a two-dimensional plane, return exactly `k` input occurrences closest to the origin `(0,0)`, in any order.

Distance is the straight-line length to the origin, `sqrt(x*x + y*y)`. Count separate input occurrences at identical coordinates separately. If points tie at the selection boundary, choose any sufficient number of tied occurrences.

## Example

Input: `points = [[1,3],[-2,2]], k = 1`

Output: `[[-2,2]]`

## Constraints

* `1 <= k <= points.length`.
* Each point has two integer coordinates, which may be negative or zero; points may repeat.
initialCode: class Solution { public int[][] kClosest(int[][] points, int k) { return new int[0][0]; } }

solutions.name: Max Heap of Size k
solutions.description:
## Approach

Maintain a max heap ordered by squared distance. Push each point into the heap, and whenever the heap grows beyond `k`, remove the farthest kept point. At the end, the heap contains exactly `k` closest candidates.

## Key Insight

A size-k max heap lets the current farthest kept point act as the boundary. Any later point closer than that boundary can replace it; any farther point can be discarded immediately.

## Complexity Analysis

Each point performs a heap operation of size at most `k`, so the time complexity is `O(n log k)`. The heap stores `O(k)` points.

solutions.name: Sort by Distance
solutions.description:
## Approach

Sort all points by squared distance from the origin and return the first `k` rows. This fully orders the input even though only the closest prefix is needed.

## Key Insight

Sorting is the simplest baseline: once distances are in ascending order, the answer is literally the first `k` points. It is useful for checking the distance formula and tie behavior.

## Complexity Analysis

Sorting costs `O(n log n)`. Java's object-array sort uses extra stack or buffer space depending on implementation details, so the auxiliary space is commonly described as `O(log n)` to `O(n)`.

solutions.name: Quickselect Partition
solutions.description:
## Approach

Partition the array by squared distance until the first `k` positions contain points whose distances are no larger than the rest. Return that prefix; the prefix does not need to be internally sorted.

## Key Insight

The task only needs the boundary between the kth closest point and the remaining points. Quickselect finds that boundary without fully sorting both sides.

## Complexity Analysis

Average time is `O(n)`, while unlucky pivots can degrade to `O(n^2)`. The partitioning is in-place, so auxiliary space is `O(1)`.

solutions.name: Min Heap of All Points
solutions.description:
## Approach

Build a min heap ordered by squared distance using every point, then poll the heap `k` times. The first `k` removals are the closest points.

## Key Insight

This route is a straightforward priority-queue baseline. It does more memory work than the size-k max heap, but it separates the idea of ordering all candidates from the optimization of keeping only k candidates.

## Complexity Analysis

Adding all points to a heap and polling `k` times costs `O(n log n + k log n)` with repeated offers, or `O(n + k log n)` with heapify. The heap stores `O(n)` points.
